claims.text: The baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy has a quasi-static yield strength of 786 MPa, compressive strength of 1314 MPa, and fracture strain of 13.5%.
Approximately 10 at.% W can be substituted into HfZrTiTa0.53.
W addition and heat treatment will create a dual-phase microstructure in the modified alloy.
The modified alloy will contain finely dispersed W-rich nanoprecipitates or secondary-phase particles at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
W promotes heterogeneous nucleation of nanoscale precipitates.
The proposed precipitates act as dislocation-pinning sites.
Precipitate pinning increases dislocation storage and restricts dislocation motion during rapid loading.
Increased dislocation storage and restricted motion enhance dynamic strain hardening.
Improved dislocation interactions and interface strengthening delay adiabatic shear localization.
Delayed shear localization increases uniform plastic deformation before failure.
The W-modified alloy will have a higher dynamic yield strength than the baseline alloy.
The W-modified alloy will exhibit greater uniform plastic deformation and a fracture strain above 13.5%.
The W-modified alloy will resist localization by delaying adiabatic shear-band formation.
The W-modified alloy will have increased impact-induced energy absorption.
The predictions apply at room temperature under adiabatic dynamic compression at strain rates of approximately 2000–3000 s^-1.
W additions improve strength and fracture strain in analogous Ti-Zr-Mo refractory alloys under quasi-static and dynamic loading.
The magnitude of the gains depends on W content and heat-treatment parameters.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome is increased energy absorption, whereas the experiment proposes impact-induced energy release measurements. Mechanical energy absorption and chemical energy release are distinct quantities and are not interchangeable.

The predicted dynamic fracture-strain improvement is framed as an increase from the 13.5% quasi-static value, while the matched experiment compares dynamically tested baseline and modified samples. The numerical quasi-static value is therefore not the matched dynamic comparator.
